newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Half dozen bids seen for Singapore telecom licence.
newsitem.headline: Half dozen bids seen for Singapore telecom licence.

text.p: As many as six groups of telecom companies are expected to register interest in licences to operate fixed-line telephone services in the Singapore market, analysts said on Tuesday.

The Singapore government said in September it would allow at least one, and possibly two, new operators to compete with state-owned telephone monopoly Singapore Telecom (SingTel) when the market is deregulated in April 2000.
To be considered for the tender, companies must register interest, or "pre-qualify", with the Telecommunication Authority of Singapore (TAS) by March 1.
Three bids have already been announced, two by Singapore consortiums, and one from Britain's Cable and Wireless.

Analysts expect at least three more foreign telecom giants to enter the fray, either with the local companies that have already announced bids or with new local players. Local firms must own at least 49 percent of each bidding group.
"I would guess there will be four to six bids...each involving a number of partners," said John Chessher, regional telecoms analyst with Schroders in Bangkok.
"The bids are likely to reflect initial investment costs of the order of S$500,000 (US$350,000) to S$1.0 billion," he said.
At first glance, Singapore's small telephone market might appear an unlikely target for the world's telecommunications giants. But analysts say it has several attractions.
Although the city-state has a resident population of only around 3.4 million, it is a key business centre for Southeast Asia and the regional headquarters for many multi-national companies.
Its population is also wealthy, with one of the world's highest penetration rates for mobile telephones and pagers.
This fact has already drawn Cable and Wireless and its unit Hong Kong Telecommunications into the market.

They have teamed up with Singapore Press Holdings (SPH) and Keppel Telecommunications and Transportation Ltd (KTT) to launch Singapore's second mobile telephone and pager service, MobileOne, from April 1 this year.
SPH and KTT said in December they would submit a joint bid for the full telecommunications licence. They have not said if it will include Cable and Wireless.

"It would make sense for Cable and Wireless to go in with their existing MobileOne partners," said Timothy Wong, telecoms analyst at brokerage Vickers Ballas. "It would offer them synergies as a full-service provider."

The other local group to announce a bid is made up of state-owned Singapore Technologies Telemedia (STT) and the state utility Singapore Power. STT said recently a successful bid could involve up to S$1 billion in infrastructure investment.
But analysts say such an investment could be easily recouped, particularly by an international telecommunications company which could use Singapore as a regional hub.

Chessher said this was likely to encourage bids from several Western companies, including British Telecom Plc and its new U.S. merger partner, MCI Communications Corp, and the Global One alliance of Sprint Corp, France Telecom and Deutsche Telekom AG.
U.S. giant AT&T could also gain from a bid, he said.
"I would be surprised if BT/MCI did not make a bid," he said. "They need an Asian leg for a global network."
